sentences.text: The holotype specimen was a subadult individual measuring approximately 3 to 4 meters in length.
This animal weighed approximately 170 to 270 kilograms.
Its basioccipital bone features very short basal tubers that reach only one-third the height of the occipital condyle.
The specific name euotica means "well-eared" because CT scans revealed a well-developed inner ear adapted for hearing low-frequency sounds.
It possessed a long cochlear duct equal in height to the labyrinth, a rare adaptation for detecting low-frequency vibrations.
The Timurlengia head is far less pneumatized than in large tyrannosaurids, suggesting air spaces in later species may have lightened the skull or aided hearing despite larger size.
Isolated tyrannosauroid bones from the Bissekty Formation were first described by Soviet researchers starting in 1944.
A neurocranium recovered in 2004 served as an anchor for neck muscles and protected the brain and ear canals.
The neurocranium was identified as a new species by Steve Brusatte in 2014 after being stored at the Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences.
The species Timurlengia euotica was named and described in 2016 by Brusatte, Averianov, Sues, Muir, and Butler.
Additional fossils referred to the species include ZIN PH 854/16, a right half of a neurocranium, and ZIN PH 676/16, a right maxilla.
These fossils were assigned to the species based on the assumption that only one tyrannosauroid taxon existed in the Bissekty Formation.
Timurlengia was likely a pursuit hunter capable of hearing low-frequency sounds due to the shape of its ear canal.
It was likely a pursuit hunter equipped with blade-like teeth for slicing meat.
Timurlengia was likely a pursuit predator with knife-shaped teeth for cutting through meat, based on preserved remains.
The robustness of Timurlengia's semicircular inner ear canals may have contributed to greater agility.
The robustness of the inner ear semicircular canals may be related to great agility.
Timurlengia had a long cochlear duct, same height as the labyrinth, an adaptation for hearing low-frequency sounds.
This may indicate the animal used low-frequency calls to communicate with other members of its species.
Timurlengia reveals that tyrannosaurs had not yet reached giant size but had already evolved key brain and sensory traits found in Late Cretaceous giants.
Although much smaller than Tyrannosaurus, the Timurlengia skull shows a sophisticated brain that likely provided keen sight, smell, and hearing.
Tyrannosaurs apparently developed large size rapidly during the Late Cretaceous, with their success as superpredators possibly facilitated by brains and senses that evolved initially in small bodies.
The neurocranium suggests tyrannosaurs likely developed advanced heads first, a hypothesis proposed by describer Hans-Dieter Sues.
Hans-Dieter Sues hypothesized that tyrannosaurs developed advanced head features before large body size, a pattern supported by Timurlengia's braincase.
Timurlengia is classified in the Tyrannosauroidea in a basal position, possibly as a sister species to Xiongguanlong.
Timurlengia is placed in the superfamily Tyrannosauroidea in a basal position as a possible sister taxon to Xiongguanlong.
The parent group for Timurlengia is Tyrannosauroidea.
Timurlengia is classified in the class Reptilia.
Together they appear to represent a clade of long-snouted forms that could be the group closest to the family Tyrannosauridae.
Timurlengia lived during the early Late Cretaceous (Turonian age) in the Kyzylkum Desert of Uzbekistan.
Timurlengia was found in Uzbekistan within the Bissekty Formation of the Kyzylkum Desert, dating to the Turonian age of the mid-Cretaceous.
The time range for Timurlengia is the Turonian stage, from 93.9 to 89.8 million years ago.
The discovery of Timurlengia filled a gap in the fossil record between small marginal hunters and large superpredators.
It is debated whether specimen ZIN PH 2330/16 belongs to Timurlengia, as Voris et al. (2025) suggested it might be a dromaeosaurid instead.
